milestones.title: Estácio de Sá founds the city
milestones.detail: On 1 March 1565 the Portuguese under Estácio de Sá landed on an isthmus between Morro Cara de Cão and Sugarloaf and founded São Sebastião do Rio de Janeiro.

milestones.title: French expelled; city moved to Morro do Castelo
milestones.detail: After the final defeat of the French in January 1567 the settlement was re-established on top of Morro do Castelo, in what is now the city centre.

milestones.title: French squadron under Duguay-Trouin takes the city
milestones.detail: In September 1711 a French squadron under René Duguay-Trouin raided the port during the War of the Spanish Succession; the Portuguese defenders were unable to hold the city.

milestones.title: Carioca Aqueduct completed
milestones.detail: The two-storey arcade of 42 arches, 270 m long and up to 17.6 m high, was inaugurated to bring fresh water from the Carioca river to the city.

milestones.title: Capital of the State of Brazil
milestones.detail: Rio de Janeiro replaced Salvador as the viceregal seat of Portuguese Brazil, as the port for the gold of Minas Gerais.

milestones.title: Portuguese royal court arrives
milestones.detail: With the transfer of the Portuguese court to Brazil, Rio became the seat of the monarchy; the population rose from about 43,000 in 1799 to about 112,000 in 1821.

milestones.title: Capital of independent Brazil
milestones.detail: After independence Rio de Janeiro served as capital of the Empire of Brazil until 1889 and then of the republic.

milestones.title: Dom Pedro II Railway opens
milestones.detail: The first section of the Estrada de Ferro Dom Pedro II and its terminal station (today Central do Brasil) were inaugurated on 29 March 1858.

milestones.title: Pereira Passos reforms and the Vaccine Revolt
milestones.detail: Mayor Pereira Passos, appointed in 1902, cut new avenues through the centre and demolished its tenements; compulsory vaccination triggered a week of rioting on 10-16 November 1904.

milestones.title: Morro do Castelo razed
milestones.detail: The hill on which the city had stood since 1567 was demolished in 1921-22 and its earth used for landfill in Guanabara Bay.

milestones.title: Christ the Redeemer dedicated
milestones.detail: The 30 m statue (38 m with pedestal) on the summit of Corcovado was dedicated on 12 October 1931.

milestones.title: Capital moves to Brasília
milestones.detail: Rio ceased to be the national capital and Federal District and became the city-state of Guanabara; in the same year's census São Paulo overtook it as Brazil's most populous city.

milestones.title: Rio–Niterói Bridge opens
milestones.detail: The 13.29 km bridge across Guanabara Bay opened on 4 March 1974.

milestones.title: Guanabara merged into Rio de Janeiro state
milestones.detail: A presidential decree known as 'the Fusion' merged the city-state with the State of Rio de Janeiro, made the city the state capital in place of Niterói and established the metropolitan region.

milestones.title: Metro begins operating
milestones.detail: The Rio de Janeiro Metro began operation on 5 March 1979.

milestones.title: Summer Olympics and Paralympics
milestones.detail: Rio hosted the 2016 Games, the first held in South America.

notes: Start date: 1 March 1565 (Estácio de Sá's settlement at the foot of Sugarloaf) is the documented founding and is not contested; Europeans first encountered Guanabara Bay on 1 January 1502 and the French built Fort Coligny on an island in the bay in 1555 (English Wikipedia's infobox lists 1555 as the first European settlement), but neither is the Portuguese city itself. The settlement was moved to Morro do Castelo in 1567; that hill was razed in 1921-22, so the historic core point marks its former site in today's Centro. Population: nothing could be sourced for 1565-1653. The 1654 figure is from a 1914 travel-history book and the 1700, 1750 and 1808 values are Chandler's estimates. From 1799 the series rests on the censuses summarised in the 1906 census volume (primary source, read in the IBGE digital library). Definitions change: 1799 covers the urban parishes only, while 1821 onward cover the whole municipality (later Federal District) including suburban and rural parishes; the urban-only figures are given in the point notes. The 1849 count (266,466) is higher than both 1838 and 1870 and conflicts with published estimates for 1850 (Chandler 166,419; Encyclopedia of Latin American History and Culture 186,000), so the series is not monotonic there; it is recorded as the census gave it. The 1856 count (151,776) is omitted because the 1906 volume notes that it is missing whole parishes. For 1872 the IBGE table gives 274,972 and the 1906 volume 266,831. The 1900 census of the city was cancelled; the 811,443 that IBGE's table prints under 1900 is the 1906 municipal census and is recorded at 1906. The 1872, 1920 and 1940 values were read from Wikipedia's transcription of the IBGE table because the IBGE page itself returned HTTP 403. Landmarks: tower heights and years are from CTBUH (which dates the Central do Brasil tower to 1945; the station building was inaugurated in 1943). CTBUH also lists the Palácio Duque de Caxias (1941) at 170 m, which looks implausible for a building of that date and is left out. Left out for lack of a sourced height: Mosteiro de São Bento, Paço Imperial, Theatro Municipal, Maracanã Stadium, the colonial forts and the Museum of Tomorrow. The Candelária height and the aqueduct height come from Wikipedia without a further citation.
